messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 55
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Farmer
  trauma_type: Assault
  pcl5: 76

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Somatic (Heart Racing): Own heart racing or pounding, Olfactory (Sweat/Body): Sweat or body odour, Perceived Threat: People acting suspiciously
  Maladaptive Strategies: Rumination: Revenge: ruminate about how to get even with assailant, Avoid Anniversaries: Dates or anniversaries connected to the event, Overworking: I throw myself into work or tasks to keep my mind occupied
  Memory: Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together, Memory Feels Alien: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me, Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Khalil's Vigil

Khalil Mansour was fifty-five years old when a man he had hired to help with seasonal work turned on him in the barn. It was late afternoon in October, the light already dimming through the gaps in the wooden slats, when the worker—someone Khalil had known casually for two seasons—suddenly produced a knife and demanded money. Khalil, a sturdy man accustomed to the physical demands of his farm in rural Pennsylvania, had tried to reason with him first. When that failed, he resisted. The man was younger, faster. Khalil remembered the initial shock of the blade, the burning sensation, but what came after fragmented into pieces that would not cohere. He remembered the smell of his own sweat, acrid and unfamiliar, mixing with the metallic scent of blood and dust. He remembered the man's face, but not clearly—it kept shifting in his mind's eye, sometimes angry, sometimes blank. He remembered falling, his palms scraping concrete, but he could not quite place where the concrete was or how he had gotten there. The ambulance arrived. Stitches. The police. But the sequence felt borrowed from someone else's story, something he had read rather than lived.

The assault had left him with physical scars that healed reasonably well. The psychological aftermath was slower to surface. For the first few weeks, Khalil had thrown himself into work with an intensity that alarmed his wife, Yasmine. He would be in the fields before dawn and would not come inside until dark, pushing through tasks that did not need pushing, reorganizing the equipment shed for the third time, scrubbing the barn floor until his hands bled. Yasmine understood this as a coping mechanism—he was a man who had always solved problems through labor—but she also noticed that he would not speak about what had happened. When she asked, he would start to explain and then lose the thread of his own narrative. "He came in, and I—" he would begin, then pause, his jaw tightening, unable to continue. It was as though the memory belonged to someone else entirely, something he had witnessed rather than endured.

By the following October, the anniversary month, Khalil became noticeably withdrawn. He had begun to avoid the barn in the weeks leading up to the date, delegating tasks to his son-in-law, something he had never done before. The avoidance extended further: he would not drive past the intersection where the police car had first turned onto his property; he would not listen to the news; he had stopped attending the mosque's Friday gatherings, claiming he was too tired. What Yasmine did not know was that Khalil was ruminating constantly about the assailant—where he was now, whether he had been released from prison, what Khalil would do if he saw him again. He had fantasies of confrontation, of evening the score, scenarios that played out in his head as he lay awake at night. These thoughts were shameful to him; they contradicted his faith and his nature, yet he could not stop them.

The real crisis came when Khalil's heart began to race unpredictably. A sudden acceleration would seize him—his pulse pounding in his ears, his chest tight—and he would become convinced that something terrible was about to happen. His own body had become a trigger. The sensation of his heart racing reminded him of the assault, though he could not articulate why or how. When his neighbor stopped by to discuss crop rotation and stood too close, Khalil felt his pulse spike. When a new hand was hired to help with the harvest, Khalil watched him with an intensity that bordered on paranoia, reading threat into casual movements, into the way the man wiped sweat from his brow.

It was Yasmine who finally insisted he see someone. She had found him in the barn at three in the morning, sitting alone in the dark, and when she asked what he was doing, he could not answer. He had come to believe that something was fundamentally broken in him, that the man who had attacked him had left him permanently fractured. When his family doctor referred him to a therapist, Khalil agreed, though he carried deep doubt that talking would help him reassemble a memory that felt as though it had never truly been his own.
